beliefs.practice: Read the Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB API) connection string from an environment-backed config (.env or config file) at startup and fail fast with a clear error message if it's missing or malformed; never hard-code or commit the secret into source control.

Reuse a single MongoClient across the whole Node.js process (singleton) and rely on connection pooling instead of creating a new client per request; configure maxPoolSize (e.g. 50–200) to match expected concurrency.
Enforce TLS in the connection string (e.g., tls=true or ssl=true) and verify server certificates to protect the connection string and data in transit.

Do bulk inserts for the ingest script: send documents in chunks (e.g., 500–2000 docs per bulkWrite) and throttle between batches to avoid RU/throughput throttling; implement exponential backoff on transient failures.

When seeding embeddings, validate and enforce a fixed embedding dimension (e.g., 1536) and reject or pad/trim inconsistent vectors before storing; store the dimension as metadata in the products collection.
Normalize embeddings to unit length when using cosine similarity (i.e., divide vector by its L2 norm before storing or before query) to make cosine or dot-product comparisons consistent.

Create a vector index on the products.embedding field with an appropriate indexType (DiskANN as available) and specify the embedding dimension and metric (e.g., metric: 'cosine'); set a query-time efSearch (or equivalent) to trade accuracy vs latency.

When the vector index supports parameters, tune search-time parameter efSearch (or scan_k/ef) to meet the recall/latency target (e.g., raise efSearch for better recall); persist the chosen value in config and document the recall/latency observed.
Store embeddings as a consistent numeric array type (prefer float32 sized values) and avoid mixed numeric types; validate types at ingest to keep index behavior predictable.

Use a two-stage recommendation pipeline: (1) ANN vector search to produce a candidate set (e.g., top 100), (2) re-rank candidates using co-purchase frequency and session memory (server-side aggregation where possible) before returning top 5.

Create efficient indexes to support co-purchase queries: on orders collection have compound indexes such as { productId: 1, orderId: 1 } and { customerId: 1, timestamp: -1 } to enable fast aggregation of co-purchases and recent activity.
Use server-side aggregation pipelines (e.g., $match, $unwind, $group, $sort, $limit) to compute co-purchase counts and session aggregation rather than pulling large amounts of data to the app.

Persist per-session memory in a dedicated sessions collection with a TTL index (expireAfterSeconds) for ephemeral memory and index sessionId as unique; keep session documents small (ids and short vectors or references).

Respect rate limiting and throttling: handle 429 responses by reading Retry-After headers (or SDK-provided retry metadata), back off and retry with exponential jitter, and surface meaningful errors to the caller if retries fail.
Limit the projection returned by queries (project only the fields you need, e.g., productId, title, price, embeddingExists flag) to reduce RU consumption and network bandwidth.

Instrument RU and latency metrics in the app (log RU charges returned in response metadata) and validate index plans (explain) in development so that queries are RU-efficient before running large-scale ingestion or search.

For development and CI when OpenAI keys are not present, use deterministic synthetic embeddings (fixed RNG seed) to make tests reproducible and validate end-to-end behavior without external API calls; guard real API usage behind an env flag.

Provide a graceful fallback if the vector index or vector query fails (e.g., index not present): return top co-purchased/popularity-based recommendations and log the missing-index condition for remediation.

Avoid long-lived transactions for recommendation flows—use idempotent single-document writes or small multi-document operations; if cross-document consistency is required, keep transactions short and rare.

Enforce uniqueness with unique indexes for primary keys used by the app (productId, sessionId) to prevent duplicates during concurrent seed runs; use upserts carefully when idempotent seeding is required.

When creating vector indexes, document the index’s storage/compute cost and perform an index-building dry-run on a small subset; avoid rebuilding very large indexes frequently—prefer incremental updates where supported.

Protect API keys used for external LLM/embedding services (OPENAI_API_KEY) the same way as DB secrets, and avoid embedding raw user or personally identifiable data in embeddings sent to third-party services unless policy-reviewed.
